summary: This document describes the style conventions and editorial policies the RFC Editor uses for the RFC Series. It covers how an RFC should be structured and written, and points to a website with extra, more experimental guidance. It replaces earlier style guidance.

eli5.summary: Every school paper has rules about headings and formatting. This RFC is the rulebook for how the people who publish RFCs expect documents to look and read.

subtitle: The RFC Editor's rules for how an RFC is written, structured and cited.

tldr.problem: RFCs come from many authors and streams, yet readers expect documents that are readable, clear, consistent and reasonably uniform.
tldr.mechanism: The Style Guide sets out the RFC Editor's basic conventions for language, punctuation, capitalization, citations and abbreviations, the required and optional parts of an RFC and their order, and the exact format of references.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2223 and is updated by RFC 7997. Newer, more experimental guidance lives on a companion website until it is ready to be folded into the guide.

today: RFC 7322 is an Informational RFC that obsoleted RFC 2223, and it is updated by RFC 7997.

sections.title: Purpose of the Style Guide
sections.content:
The goal of the RFC publication process is documents that are readable, clear, consistent, and reasonably uniform. The basic formatting conventions were set in the 1970s by the original RFC Editor, Jon Postel. This Style Guide records the fundamental and unique conventions and editorial policies currently used for the RFC Series, as a stable, infrequently updated reference for authors, editors and reviewers.

For general grammar, punctuation and capitalization the RFC Editor follows the Chicago Manual of Style, with a few exceptions to avoid ambiguity in technical prose, handle mixed text and computer languages, or preserve historical formatting. Newer issues are first handled on a web portion of the Style Guide and may join the RFC when it is revised.

All RFCs begin as Internet-Drafts, and the RFC Editor applies the Series rules during editing.
sections.eli5: RFCs have to look and read alike, so there is a rulebook. It mostly follows a normal writing guide, with a few special rules for technical writing.

sections.title: The RFC Editor's Philosophy
sections.content:
The RFC Editor aims to prepare each document in RFC style, make it as clear, consistent and readable as possible, correct larger clarity problems and flag unclear passages for the author, and fix inconsistencies such as terms that appear in different forms. Consistency is sought within the document, within a cluster of related documents, and across the Series on the same subject.

The editing is not an additional technical review. Whether a wording change affects technical meaning is for the author, working group or stream-approving body to decide, and if the original wording is more accurate technically, it takes precedence over editorial convention.

The RFC calls the tension between author and editor "editorial balance" and sets one prime directive that rules over grammar: do not change the intended meaning of the text. If a document cannot be edited without serious risk of altering its meaning, it may be returned to the stream-approving body.
sections.eli5: The editor is like a teacher fixing spelling and flow, not changing your science. If a fix would change what you meant, your meaning wins.

sections.title: Language, Punctuation and Citation Conventions
sections.content:
RFCs are published in English, and spelling may be American or British as long as one document is consistent. Punctuation rules include no overstriking or underlining, two spaces after a sentence-ending period, a comma before the last item in a series, and punctuation placed outside quotation marks when quoting literal text.

Generic example DNS names should use those reserved in BCP 32, and angle brackets around URIs are strongly recommended. Major words in titles are capitalized in title case, and capitalization must be consistent within a document.

Citations must be in square brackets, such as [CITE1], must match the references list, and tags must not contain spaces, so [RFC2119] is correct. Cross-references use section numbers, not page numbers. Abbreviations should be expanded in titles and at first use, except very common ones like TCP, IP, SNMP and HTTP.

This guide does not use RFC 2119 terminology. Lowercase "must" marks changes the RFC Editor will make automatically, and lowercase "should" marks recommendations that authors may be asked about but are not required to follow.
sections.eli5: There are small rules, like using brackets for citations and spelling out a short name the first time you use it, so every RFC feels the same to read.

sections.title: The Structure of an RFC
sections.content:
An RFC is built from a fixed sequence of parts. Outside the body of the memo the order is required; within the body the order is strongly recommended. Elements before the body are not numbered, the body has numbered sections, and appendices are lettered.

The first-page header lists authors, usually no more than five, with their organizations, and shows the ISSN 2070-1721 and any Updates or Obsoletes lines in ascending order. The title should represent scope and purpose without being too general or too long. Every RFC must have an Abstract that is concise, complete in itself and contains no citations, and a table of contents is required.

The body must have an Introduction, and uses of capitalized words like MUST must cite RFC 2119 or define their meaning. IANA Considerations are guided by BCP 26, and the RFC Editor removes an IANA section that says there are none. A Security Considerations section is required. Optional Acknowledgements and Contributors sections follow, and an Authors' Addresses section with a long-lived email address is required; munged addresses are not allowed.
sections.eli5: Every RFC has the same parts in the same order, like a recipe card: title, short summary, ingredients, steps, and who wrote it.

sections.title: How References Are Written
sections.content:
The reference list holds only entries, with no introductory text. References must be marked normative or informative, and normative ones are essential to implementing or understanding the RFC. When both exist, the list is split into Normative and Informative subsections, ordered by citation tag.

References to RFCs use a required format that depends on the number of authors. A reference to an RFC in the STD, BCP or FYI sub-series must include the sub-series number, and when a sub-series has several RFCs the entry lists all of them. Internet-Draft references may only be informative, and must give the posting date, full file name with version, and the phrase "Work in Progress". A normative reference to an Internet-Draft suspends publication until that draft is ready too. Errata are cited as [ErrNumber]. References to other standards bodies' documents use their common abbreviated names, and URIs are acceptable if stable and direct.
sections.eli5: When you list the books you used, you write them all down the same way, and you say which ones were really needed and which were just extra reading.

sections.title: Disputes, Returns and Revising the Guide
sections.content:
If an author disagrees with the RFC Production Center (RPC) over how a rule applies, they should first discuss it with the RPC. If there is no agreement, the RFC Series Editor decides, with input from the stream-approving body, and further resolution follows the process in the RFC Editor Model.

A document the RFC Editor cannot edit without risking its technical meaning, or lacks resources to edit, can be sent back to the stream-approving body to improve. This is not a dispute with the author.

The Series keeps evolving, so less formal recommendations are posted on the RFC Editor website and trialled for a period before being added to the Style Guide or kept informal. The RFC states that it has no security considerations.
sections.eli5: If you and the editor disagree about a rule, you talk first, and then someone senior makes the final call. New ideas are tried out on a website before they become real rules.
